extracted.intended_audience: state regulators, power sector stakeholders (plant owners/operators), environmental and energy industry commenters, and environmental lawyers/advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and regulatory rationale establishing BSER determinations and degrees of emission limitation for existing and new steam generating units and combustion turbine EGUs under CAA section 111, including treatment of coal-, natural gas-, and oil-fired units and legal defenses against MQD challenges. Addresses technical, economic, and programmatic factors used to select or reject candidate controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for intermediate and base load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing BSER for intermediate and base load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units to be routine methods of operation and maintenance, such that the sources could maintain the emission rates (on a lb/MWh-gross basis) currently maintained by the majority of the fleet across discrete ranges of annual capacity factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: adequately demonstrated because units already operate with those practices; no or negligible additional costs (no new technology required); no adverse non-air quality health/environmental impacts or adverse energy impacts; prevents increases in emission rates. Applies regardless of the operating horizon of the unit. Degree of emission limitation associated with this BSER is 'no increase in emission rate on a lb CO2/MWh-gross basis over an extended period of time (e.g., a year)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for low load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units — uniform fuels
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a BSER of uniform fuels for low load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units, with presumptive standards depending on fuel type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: high variability in emission rates at low-load makes an lb CO2/MWh-gross standard unreliable; a heat-input basis is reasonable. Degree of emission limitation (presumptive standard) is fixed on a heat-input basis: 130 lb CO2/MMBtu for natural gas-fired steam generating units and 170 lb CO2/MMBtu for oil-fired steam generating units. Draws on prior use of heat-input based fuel composition ('clean fuels' in 2015 NSPS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Rate Improvements (HRI) are not BSER for (existing) coal-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not finalizing HRI as part of the BSER for any subcategory of existing coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons and evidence: HRI measures typically yield small unit-level CO2 emission rate reductions (generally 0.1 to 5 percent; most measures <1 percent; some up to ~5.15%), many HRI have limited applicability or have already been applied, different HRI combinations do not necessarily produce additive reductions, some measures only affect net-generation/basis and not gross-basis emission rates. Overall expected fleet-average reductions are small relative to CCS or natural gas co-firing. Prior rulemakings (CPP, ACE) considered HRI and found limited applicability and modest regional averages. Because reductions are small and HRI can induce rebound effects, EPA concluded HRI is not BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebound effect as a disqualifying consideration for candidate controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductions achieved on a rate basis from HRI may not result in overall emission reductions and could instead cause a 'rebound effect' from increased utilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: improved heat rate lowers variable operating costs, making a unit more competitive and potentially increasing output; increased output can offset or exceed per-unit emission-rate reductions, yielding no net decrease (or an increase) in total CO2. EPA considered rebound risk in prior rules (CPP, ACE) and uses potential for perverse GHG outcomes as a basis to reject HRI where rebound is plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory BSER factors (CAA section 111(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: BSER determinations must be based on the factors in CAA section 111(a)(1): adequate demonstration, costs of control (reasonable cost), and emissions reductions achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA applies these criteria when evaluating candidate controls (e.g., found CCS for long-term coal-fired units meets these factors: adequately demonstrated, of reasonable cost, and achieves substantial emissions reductions). Analysis includes technical demonstration, cost analysis, and quantification of emissions benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Major Questions Doctrine concerns — reliance on 'traditional add-on pollution controls'
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid MQD challenges, BSER selections should be consistent with 'traditional, add-on emissions control' approaches that focus on improving performance of individual sources rather than 'generation-shifting' approaches that reconfigure the overall power system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's defense: CCS is characterized as an add-on control reducing emissions at individual sources (not an unprecedented generation-shifting approach). The distinction matters legally under West Virginia v. EPA; generation-shifting as BSER was found problematic by the Court, whereas add-on controls have historical precedent and are consistent with statutory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/qualification of HRI measures versus routine maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: HRI measures are distinct from regular practices that recover degradation but do not upgrade heat rate beyond recent design levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: HRI measures include boiler island improvements (neural network system, intelligent sootblower), steam turbine overhaul/upgrades, and equipment upgrades (variable frequency drives). Regular, non-HRI practices include in-kind replacements and routine surface cleaning (descaling, fouling removal); those do not constitute HRI because they do not produce heat rate upgrades beyond recent design levels. Some HRI measures only affect net-generation basis and thus might not show on gross-basis emission rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of economic incentives, tax credits, and evolving markets in BSER feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic supports (e.g., IRC section 45Q tax credit) and potential CO2 utilization markets significantly affect the affordability and operational viability of controls like CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes 45Q tax credit reduces CCS capital/operating cost and can incentivize increased generation by CCS-equipped units; projections of retirements or CCS adoption depend on such incentives. EPA will monitor economic developments (cost declines, CO2 markets) when assessing rule impacts and BSER feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory commitment to periodic review and potential revision (timebound review)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is committing to review and, if appropriate, revise the requirements of this rule by January 1, 2041.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the 12-year availability of IRC 45Q tax credit, potential growth of CO2 utilization markets, state decarbonization measures, and technological/economic changes may materially affect CCS economics and compliance feasibility. The commitment is codified in the regulations to allow states and EPA to reconsider standards before/around expiration of key incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determinations for new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbine EGUs (subcategories)
rubrics_metrics.description: For stationary combustion turbine EGUs commencing construction or reconstruction after May 23, 2023, EPA finalizes BSER determinations by subcategory: low load turbines — use of lower-emitting fuels; intermediate load turbines — highly efficient simple cycle generation; base load turbines — BSER includes two components corresponding initially to a two-phase standard of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These BSER determinations are codified in 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa and reflect technology/operational distinctions among simple cycle and combined cycle technologies and load-based subcategories (low, intermediate, base). Section VIII.C–G provide further discussion of applicability, technology, and standards of performance for each subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heat-input based fuel composition ('uniform fuels') as a valid BSER approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat-input based fuel composition (termed 'clean fuels' in prior rulemakings) can serve as BSER, especially for low-load sources where lb/MWh metrics are impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA previously used heat-input based fuel composition as BSER in the 2015 NSPS for certain turbines. For low-load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units and for low-load combustion turbines, lower-emitting fuels specified on a heat-input basis are a reasonable BSER due to greater stability for compliance measurement at variable loads.
